:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we would like to find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=2\cos{t}, \quad y=2\sin{t}
$$

from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as shown below.

![](images/83/836757696669a0852812a63c8cafcf9ac3bddd73558f7b3e67c8427ec39c008a.png)

It can be shown that the arc length $L$ of a curve defined parametrically by

$$
x=x(t), \quad y=y(t), \qquad t\in [t_1,t_2],
$$

is given by the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\,\textrm{d}t.
$$

The intuition behind this formula is given at the end of this tutorial.

According to the formula, the length of the blue arc is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}t))}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}t))}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{sin}t)}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}t+{cos}^{2}t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\,\text{d}t \\  & =2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =2(\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/83/834eff403ac2a6f696e104ec914cac1b951f8a6d989e11c0e9f2576ac9e7f0d8.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=1-t, \quad y= \dfrac{2}{3} t^{3/2}, \qquad t\in[0,1].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)=-1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{3}{t}^{3/2})={t}^{1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{{(-1)}^{2}+{({t}^{1/2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{1+t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the expression that gives the length of the curve defined by the parametric equations
$x=t, \, y=\ln{(\cos{t})}$
from $t=0$ to $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ (see graph below).

![](images/48/48de26c11ae08afb45ec19ee56e770f7418f9be2afb8ee7dd46a0d1136cb125b.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To compute the arc length $L$ of a parametrically defined curve, we use the formula

$$
L = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t}\right)^2}\:\textrm{d}t.
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡t))=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(1)}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+{tan}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sec}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve Containing Special Functions

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find the arc length of the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=e^t(\cos{t}+\sin{t}), \quad y=e^t(\cos{t}-\sin{t}) , \quad t\in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right].
$$

![](images/15/15d185178bf8882f837c19361d630c0e537e145ca2337cad4655677255d0348a.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Computing the derivatives of $x$ and $y,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)) \\  & ={e}^{t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+{e}^{t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute these derivatives in the formula for arc length, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}+{(-2{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{4{e}^{2t}({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}2{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{e}^{t}{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =2({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Arc Length of a Parametric Curve

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's go back to our first example, which was to find the arc length of the curve defined by

$$
x=2\cos{t}, \quad y=2\sin{t}, \quad t\in\left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right].
$$

![](images/83/836757696669a0852812a63c8cafcf9ac3bddd73558f7b3e67c8427ec39c008a.png)

First, we divide the interval $\left[ 0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right]$ into small subintervals of equal length. Consider a part of the blue arc that corresponds to one of those subintervals and let the length of that part be $\Delta{s}$.

![](images/35/3502e1055e3c22ef338dcfa015a4d603f808e9db5d3afea75391edddb440801a.png)

We can now denote the horizontal displacement as $\Delta{x}$ and the vertical shift as $\Delta{y}.$ 

![](images/ed/ed47d9cb8d8bce8514bc876870a5f3e175a87d2e59817ddbb3e10fd8094b24d3.png)

To approximate the length $\Delta{s}$ we apply the Pythagorean theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Δs & \approx \sqrt{{(Δx)}^{2}+{(Δy)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To approximate the total length $L,$ we need to sum up all of the little $\Delta s$ terms, so

$$
L \approx \sum \Delta s = \sum \sqrt{\left( \Delta{x} \right)^2 + \left( \Delta{y} \right)^2}.
$$

We then take the limit as $\Delta x, \Delta y \rightarrow 0.$ As we do this, the sum becomes a definite integral, and our approximation approaches the exact value of $L$. So, using the chain rule, we arrive at

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =\int \sqrt{{(\text{d}x)}^{2}+{(\text{d}y)}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \text{d}t)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\cdot \text{d}t)}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}\cdot {(\text{d}t)}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}\cdot {(\text{d}t)}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{\text{d}{t}^{2}} \\  & ={\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
